title: Fast Surface Tension Measurement of Liquid Iron and 304L Steel Using an Aerodynamic Levitation Apparatus and a New Multi-burst Excitation
abstract: Abstract Liquid metals play a crucial role in strategic industrial processes such as additive manufacturing, casting, and welding. Accurate knowledge of their physicochemical properties, particularly surface tension, is essential for process optimization. This work presents a fast-multi-burst acoustic excitation method applied through a loudspeaker in an aerodynamic levitation setup for determining the surface tension of high-purity iron (99.95 %) and 304L stainless steel. The method is based on oscillating droplet resonance and the Rayleigh theoretical framework. The multi-burst excitation enables the acquisition of multiple dynamic responses from a single experiment, providing several independent surface tension measurements on the same sample. Successive acoustic bursts, delivered at short time intervals, induce oscillations from which only the free vibration phases are analyzed. To improve frequency identification and observe frequency splitting during successive bursts, a time frequency analysis using spectrograms is employed in addition to Fourier transform processing. Surface tension measurements obtained for iron (1 605 °C to 1 996 °C) and 304L stainless steel (1 604 °C to 2 185 °C) show good agreement with literature data. The proposed multi-burst acoustic excitation technique is therefore a rapid, contamination-free, and reliable method for determining the surface tension of liquid metals at very high temperatures.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Liquid metals play an essential role in many strategic industries such as transport (automotive, maritime, aeronautics), nuclear power, and the steel industry. They are involved in shaping and manufacturing processes such as metal additive manufacturing, casting, and welding. In this global industrial context, precise knowledge of the properties of metals in the liquid state, in particular surface tension, is crucial for controlling and improving these processes [ 1 ]. For instance, the variation of the surface tension with temperature influences the final shape of the solidified object, such as a weld or ingot, as it induces fluid motion [ 2 ]. The measurement of the surface tension of liquid pure iron and steels is therefore essential but remains challenging due to data dispersion, experimental constraints, and the wide diversity of industrial alloys.

Surface tension of liquid metals can be measured using contact [ 3 ,  4 ] and non-contact techniques [ 2 ]. Among contact methods, the sessile and pendant drop techniques determine surface tension by analyzing the droplet shape governed by the balance between gravity and capillary forces [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 – 8 ]. These approaches have been successfully applied to refractory metals and alloys at high temperatures, generally with uncertainties around 5 %, but their accuracy can be affected by thermal gradients, droplet oscillations, and contamination due to interactions with substrates or containers [ 5 ,  6 ]. Another widely used technique is the maximum bubble pressure (MBP) method, where the pressure required to form a gas bubble through a capillary is related to surface tension [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]. This method has been applied to complex melts and metallic alloys over wide temperature ranges, although measurement accuracy may still be influenced by capillary immersion conditions, temperature gradients, and viscous effects in high-viscosity liquids [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]. In general, contact techniques remain sensitive to contamination because surface tension is strongly affected by impurities [ 2 ,  12 ]. To overcome these limitations, non-contact methods such as the oscillating drop technique under levitation provide more reliable measurements by eliminating interactions with solid surfaces [ 2 ].

Non-contact techniques used to determine the surface tension of liquid metals mainly rely on levitation methods such as electrostatic levitation (ESL) [ 13 ], electromagnetic levitation (EML) [ 14 ], and aerodynamic levitation (ADL) [ 15 ]. In ESL, the sample is electrically charged and stabilized in an electric field, allowing precise thermophysical measurements at high temperatures with uncertainties typically below 5 %, although residual motion or evaporation can affect accuracy [ 16 ,  17 – 18 ]. EML uses alternating magnetic fields to levitate and heat conductive samples, but induced sample motion and deformation may complicate measurements, requiring careful analysis of droplet oscillations to determine surface tension [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ]. Aerodynamic levitation offers greater versatility because it imposes fewer constraints on material properties and can levitate both metallic and dielectric samples [ 22 ,  23 ]. Using this approach, the surface tension of liquid silicon was successfully determined from oscillation frequencies of levitated droplets heated by a CO 2  laser over a wide temperature range, showing good agreement with other levitation studies and highlighting the advantages of contactless measurements in avoiding contamination effects [ 24 ].

Only the free oscillations associated with each response are analyzed for the determination of the surface tension. Moreover, the short duration of excitations and the resulting free oscillations (< 2 s) helps limit the total test duration thereby reducing high-temperature evaporation. The second major contribution of this work concerns the time frequency analysis, performed using a spectrogram, to observe the lifting of degeneracy. This temporal tracking of frequency splitting enhances the interpretation of the Fourier spectrum. The study was carried out on high-purity iron (99.95 %) and 304L stainless steel. This article first describes the oscillating drop method and the experimental setup, then presents the multi-burst acoustic excitation and the time frequency analysis. Finally, the surface tension results are reported, together with an uncertainty evaluation and a comparison with literature data.

sections.heading: Oscillating Drop Method
Experimental Setup
paragraphs: The experimental setup (Fig.  2 ) used for the surface tension measurements has the following characteristics. The sample is levitated by pure argon jet (Air Liquid Alpha Gaz 2) injected through a copper nozzle (60° convergent divergent), with the assembly placed in a sealed 316L stainless steel chamber (150 mm side), allowing atmosphere control. Fig. 2 Experimental setup of aerodynamic levitated oscillating droplet

The gas flow is regulated by Brooks SLA5860 numerical flowmeters, ensuring the supply of the chamber and the levitation. Heating is provided by an IPG-Photonics YLR-QCW laser (wavelength  λ  = 1 070 nm) with a maximal power of 300 W. The temperature of the sample is measured using an Optris CT-Ratio bichromatic pyrometer (wavelengths 900 nm and 1 050 nm), covering a range of 600 °C to 3 000 °C. The excitation of the sample is performed by an acoustic perturbation generated by an amplifier driving a standard loudspeaker, in a frequency range between 170 Hz and 300 Hz. Droplet oscillations are recorded using a high-speed camera Phantom VEO-310L, operating at 2 kHz in this study, with dual visualization (top and side views, Fig.  3 ) obtained with a dedicated mirrors system. Fig. 3 Side and top views of the levitated droplet recorded by the high-speed camera through the mirror set

sections.heading: Experimental Procedure
paragraphs: The sample is cut from an iron rod and then stored in acetone to prevent oxidation. The square samples have a mass ranging from 29.00 mg to 34.00 mg, measured with a Mettler Toledo XS205DI balance (precision of the average based on three measurements: 0.01 mg). The sample is then placed on the nozzle, the levitation chamber is sealed, and the devices are switched on. The air is removed from the chamber using a vacuum pump until the pressure is below 1 mbar. Then, the chamber is refilled with argon. The process is repeated twice to ensure the absence of oxygen. Oxygen controls ensure a residual O 2  of less than 5 ppm. A pre-melting stage allows the sample to adopt a spherical shape, prior to the launch of the automated temperature control using a MATLAB homemade software. The amplifier generates the acoustic waves responsible for the sample oscillations with a specific excitation detailed in the next part, and the evolution of the shape of the droplet is recorded by the high-speed camera based on two views. Video processing involves the simultaneous analysis of axial and lateral views (Fig.  3 ). An elliptical approximation of the droplet shape is applied frame by frame to obtain on both views: perpendicular radii ( x T ,  y T  on top view and  x S ,  y S  on side view) and the disk surface (projected area) over time. Finally, the resonant frequency is assessed through an FFT on all the radii and surfaces.

sections.heading: Multi-burst Excitation Method for Droplet Oscillations Analysis
paragraphs: In this work, the excitation of the sample is achieved through a sequence of successive acoustic burst separated by controlled resting intervals (Fig.  4 a). Each burst consists of a multifrequency acoustic signal formed by the superposition of five sinusoidal components. A reference frequency is chosen close to the expected resonance frequency. The four remaining frequencies correspond to offsets of ± 10 Hz and ± 20 Hz from the reference expected frequency. Fig. 4 (a) Multi–burst frequency excitation method to excite the same sample multiple times and observe its natural response. (b) Temporal evolution of the different radii

All the five frequencies are played simultaneously giving a kind of white noise. During the first burst (typically 0.2 s), the sample is set into oscillation by the loudspeaker, and during the subsequent pause (typically 1.5 s), it is allowed to freely relax back to its equilibrium state. This excitation and relaxation sequence are repeated several times within a single experiment, allowing the sample to be excited multiple times. This excitation is reproduced up to 5 times with a time at the liquid state < 10 s for low temperatures (< 2000 °C). When high temperature is reached (> 2000 °C), the number of excitation is reduced to 2, limiting the time at liquid state < 5 in order to preserve the chemical composition from evaporation. In all cases, the analysis focuses exclusively on the free response of the sample, once the acoustic signal is switched off. Indeed, the excitation is perturbed by the five frequencies, whereas the relaxation is assumed to be close to the natural response of the sample. Figure  4 b shows the temporal evolution of the sample radii, obtained using multi-burst acoustic excitation, specifically those measured in the side and top views (Fig.  3 ).

This approach offers several significant advantages. First, it enables the study of the intrinsic dynamic of the system without the influence of the external forces, thus ensuring that only the natural behavior of the sample is analyzed. Moreover, the repetition of multiple excitation cycles within a single test provides several successive free responses, allowing multiple estimations of the surface tension for the same sample. Finally, the short duration of the measurement sequence helps to minimize the evaporation of the molten metal or volatile alloying elements, thereby reducing measurement uncertainty.

To observe frequency splitting and perhaps facilitate the identification of each peak, we combine classical FFT analysis with a time frequency analysis using a spectrogram (Fig.  5 a). The FFT is performed over each free oscillation period (Fig.  5 b and c), lasting 1.5 s. No difference is observed between the frequency spectra obtained at the beginning and at the end of the damping phase, supporting the consistency of the sample’s natural response. Within this short time, not all degeneracies split. Immediately after the first excitation, a single degenerate characteristic frequency is observed (Fig.  5 b). During subsequent periods, several peaks become visible (Fig.  5 c); however, they cannot be clearly assigned based on the radii difference and the projected surface, possibly due to a rotation of the sample about axes other than symmetry axis. The temporal frequency analysis, performed using the side and top views and based on the evolution of the radii along the  x  and  y  axes, together with the surface analysis presented in Fig.  6 , makes it possible to precisely observe the evolution of frequencies. This time–frequency analysis clearly highlights a progressive split of the frequencies over time in the side and top views for the radii along  x . Similarly, the surface analysis associated with these two views confirms this observation, contrary to the analyses conducted along the  y  axes. This processing enables us to reveal certain peaks that are sometimes not perceptible in the views, while others are clearly observable. However, here again, comparing the radii difference and the projected surface (area top) does not allow for a clear peak assignment. Nevertheless, the classical FFT analysis and spectrograms show that the first free oscillation period, corresponding to a degenerate characteristic frequency, can be used to determine the surface tension directly from Eq.  2  with high confidence. Fig. 6 Temporal evolution of frequencies for different views of the sample

We can observe on Fig.  5 a that frequencies are splitting gradually with time. This behavior is poorly reproducible and can result from instabilities or uncontrolled rotation. Except for the fi rst burst, when splitting occurs, and giving previous discussion, the confidence is lower and force to introduce an arbitrary assumption for the position of the  m  = 0 mode. In this study, based on the temporal evolution shown in Fig.  5 a, we assume thatthe  m  = 0 mode remains at the central value, assuming a symetric frequency spliting as observed in Refs. [ 34 ,  35 ].

sections.heading: Uncertainties
paragraphs: The measurement uncertainty on the mass is established by a statistical evaluation (type A) using calibrated standard weights and amounts to 0.01 mg. For pure iron, the uncertainty on the frequency is estimated from a set of four measurements performed at nearly identical temperature and mass, namely within ± 15 °C and ± 0.7 mg, respectively. The uncertainty on the surface tension is then calculated using Eq.  6 . Overall, considering all the performed measurements, the maximum uncertainty on the surface tension reaches 0.08 N m −1 . For 304L stainless steel, the uncertainty on the frequency is estimated again from a set of five measurements performed at nearly identical temperature and mass, namely within ± 5 °C and ± 0.8 mg, respectively, resulting in a maximum uncertainty of 0.04 N m −1  on the surface tension.

sections.heading: Surface Tension of 99.95 % Pure Iron
paragraphs:
This section presents the calculation of the surface tension of 99.95 % pure iron for samples with masses ranging from 29.00 mg to 32.00 mg, over a temperature range from 1 605 °C to 1 996 °C. Temperatures are measured using the pyrometer described in the experimental procedure section. The resulting surface tension values for pure iron are also reported in Table  1 .

The maximum uncertainty in the surface tension reaches 0.08 N m −1 , which is consistent with the observed scatter of the data.

A comparison between the surface tension values of pure iron obtained in the present study and those reported in the literature shows that most measurements were performed below 1 900 °C. Similar results above 1 900 °C have also been reported in the literature [ 35 ,  40 ]. The associated uncertainties are comparable, around 2 % [ 35 ], compared with approximately 5 % in the present work. Overall, despite differences in the experimental setups (ADL, EML, or ESL) and the purity levels of the samples, our results are in good agreement with those reported in the literature.

sections.heading: Surface Tension of 304L Stainless Steel

Following the chemical characterization, surface tension measurements are carried out using the method described in the previous sections. The surface tension of 304L stainless steel is calculated for several samples with masses ranging from 30.00 mg to 34.00 mg. Measurements were performed over a temperature range from 1 604 °C to 2 185 °C. The resonance frequencies of each sample were determined using the same formulation (3) applied in the three-peak analysis of the pure iron experiments. Figure  8  shows the surface tension results for steels with similar chemical compositions. The star-shaped markers, accompanied by vertical error bars, represent our measurements of the surface tension of 304L steel. The chemical composition of the steel, determined by SEM/EDS before and after the experiment, is reported in Table  2 . The short duration of the multi-burst acoustic excitation method significantly reduces the time spent in the liquid state, which helps to limit evaporation phenomena. Fig. 8 Surface tension of liquid 304L stainless steel, including literature data

The results show no significant change in the major elemental composition (Fe, Si, Mn, Cr, Ni) after levitation. However, some elements initially detected at low levels, such as C, N, S, and O, are not reported after the experiment. As these elements are present at concentrations close to the detection limits of the SEM/EDS technique, no definitive conclusion can be drawn regarding their stability.

The speed of the multi-burst acoustic excitation method enables us to significantly reduce analysis time, which plays a decisive role in minimizing (but not supressing) sample evaporation and preserving their initial chemical composition. Indeed, the shorter the duration of the experiment, the more effective the limitation of evaporation phenomena. The results presented in this paper are obtained over a temperature range between 1 604 °C and 2 185 °C. The maximum uncertainty on the surface tension reaches 0.04 N m⁻ 1 , which is lower than the measurement scatter.

The present results are compared with the data available in the literature, in particular those reported in [ 41 ], represented by circles in Fig.  8 . In that study, surface tension measurements are performed on SS316L containing 200 ppm sulfur (circles) and containing 10 ppm sulfur (circles). The results demonstrated that whereas dissolved sulfur in SS316L led to a decrease in surface tension. Indeed, sulfur and oxygen are considered surface-active species. These results demonstrate the influence of chemical composition specifically sulfur content on the surface tension value, thereby emphasizing the need to ensure chemical composition stability, especially during short-duration experiments.

These results are corroborated for 316L stainless steel with an initial sulfur content of 20 ppm [ 42 ]. During the experiments, the samples are levitated and maintained in the liquid state for long durations (20 min) and shorter durations. Energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) analyses performed on the levitated samples after the experiments reveal an almost complete disappearance of manganese (Mn). This observation is consistent with the evolution of Mn content reported in [ 42 ] for experimental durations of the same order of magnitude. In their long-duration liquid-state experiments (20 min), represented by diamonds in Fig.  8 , authors conclude that the surface tension measurements are not reliable due to significant changes in chemical composition, including a decrease in sulfur content and the almost complete disappearance of manganese.
Shorter experiments are also carried out (diamonds) to limit evaporation and changes in chemical composition, resulting in a final sulfur content between 15 ppm and 20 ppm.

Overall experimental uncertainties of approximately 5 % were reported [ 41 ]. These results confirm that short-duration experiments minimize sample evaporation and, consequently, limit changes in chemical composition [ 42 ]. The measurements reported in the literature, notably those presented in [ 38 ] and [ 42 ], extend up to 1700 °C. In contrast, the results of the present study cover an interval between approximately 1 604 °C and 2 185 °C. Despite the elevated temperatures investigated, the chemical composition determined before and after the experiments remains controlled (Table  2 ) likely due to the very short duration of the liquid phase (< 2 s). Good agreement is observed with the data reported in [ 41 ] within the temperature range from 1 600 °C to 1 700 °C, although the chemical compositions of 304L and 316L stainless steels are slightly different.

The surface tension measurements of pure iron and 304L steel obtained in the present study, using aerodynamic levitation combined with the oscillating drop method, are based on a rapid multi-burst acoustic excitation approach coupled with the analysis of the droplet free vibrations. This methodology incorporates time–frequency analysis through the use of a spectrogram, thereby improving the interpretation of frequency peaks obtained from the FFT. Such a combined approach has proven particularly effective in accurately identifying the principal frequency of the Fourier spectrum. The good agreement between the present results and literature data obtained using other levitation techniques, as discussed previously, and in some cases under slightly different experimental conditions, confirms the relevance and reliability of the developed methodology for measuring the surface tension of iron and steel. For pure iron, the results indicate a decrease in surface tension with increasing temperature. A similar trend is observed for 304L steel. The slightly higher values measured in this study can be attributed to specific experimental conditions. Finally, the multi-burst acoustic excitation approach, combined with rapid signal acquisition and advanced spectral analysis, demonstrates strong potential for accurate and reproducible surface tension measurements under levitation conditions. Free vibration analysis with a very short acquisition time (< 2 s) minimizes evaporation phenomena, as observed in the experiments conducted on steel presented in this article.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: A methodology based on the analysis of free vibrations of an acoustically excited levitated droplet has been developed for surface tension determination. The combined use of FFT and spectrogram analysis enabled a better understanding of resonance frequencies, even in the presence of droplet deformation and rotation. The short analysis time window (< 2 s) limited external disturbances and evaporation effects. This led to in improved measurement accuracy, reduced manganese loss, and more reliable surface tension data for stainless steel above 1 600 °C. Application to high-purity iron (99.95 %) in the temperature range from 1 605 °C to 1 996 °C and to 304L stainless steel in the range from 1 604 °C to 2 185 °C yielded results in very good agreement with literature data, confirming the reliability of the approach. The proposed contactless and reproducible method is well suited for investigating liquid metals and alloys and showed strong potential for extension to more extreme conditions and industrial applications.
